easy.text: According to Newton's first law, an object at rest will stay at rest unless:

options.text: An unbalanced force acts on it
options.feedback: Correct -- objects resist changes to their motion unless a net force pushes or pulls them.
Time passing alone doesn't change an object's motion.
Color has no effect on motion.
Observation alone doesn't apply any physical force to an object.

medium.text: What term describes an object's tendency to resist changes in its state of motion?

options.feedback: Correct -- inertia is the resistance to a change in motion, the core idea behind the first law.
Velocity describes speed and direction, not resistance to change.
Acceleration describes a change in velocity, not the resistance to that change.
Gravity is a specific force, not the general property of resisting motion changes.

hard.text: A hockey puck sliding on frictionless ice continues moving in a straight line at constant speed. This best illustrates:

options.text: Newton's first law -- no net force means no change in motion
options.feedback: Correct -- with no friction or other unbalanced force, the puck's motion stays constant, exactly as the first law predicts.

options.text: Newton's third law -- for every action there's an equal and opposite reaction
options.feedback: The third law is about paired forces between two interacting objects, not about maintaining constant motion.

options.text: The law of conservation of mass
options.feedback: That law is about matter in chemical reactions, unrelated to a puck's motion.

options.text: Newton's second law -- force equals mass times acceleration
options.feedback: The second law explains changing motion under force; here there's no force and no change, which is the first law's territory.

easy.hard: Only something applying a net push or pull can change this object's state of motion.
easy.medium: Something has to actually push or pull on it to change what it's doing.
easy.easy: A force has to act on it to make it start moving.

medium.hard: This property describes why heavier or already-moving objects resist having their motion altered.
medium.medium: This is the name for an object's built-in resistance to changing its speed or direction.
medium.easy: This is the tendency of objects to keep doing what they're already doing.

hard.hard: With friction eliminated, there's no unbalanced force acting on the puck, so its motion cannot change -- this is the defining scenario the first law describes.
hard.medium: Since there's no friction slowing it down, there's no force changing its motion, which is exactly what this law predicts.
hard.easy: With nothing pushing or slowing it down, the puck just keeps going the same way, forever -- which law describes that?

easy.text: What is the key difference between speed and velocity?

options.text: Velocity includes direction, speed does not
options.feedback: Correct -- velocity is speed with a specified direction.

options.text: Speed includes direction, velocity does not
options.feedback: This has it backwards -- velocity is the one that includes direction.

options.text: They are always the same value with no difference
options.feedback: They can have the same magnitude, but conceptually direction is what sets them apart.

options.text: Speed is measured in a different unit than velocity
options.feedback: Both are commonly measured in the same units, like meters per second -- the difference is conceptual, not unit-based.

medium.text: A car travels 100 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

options.feedback: Correct -- speed equals distance divided by time: 100/2 = 50.
This multiplies distance and time instead of dividing.
This ignores the 2-hour time period entirely.
This divides time by distance instead of distance by time.

hard.text: A runner completes one full lap around a circular track, ending up back at the starting point. Which statement is true?

options.text: Their average speed was greater than zero, but their average velocity was zero
options.feedback: Correct -- they covered real distance (positive speed), but since displacement (start to end position) is zero, velocity is zero.

options.text: Both their average speed and average velocity were zero
options.feedback: Speed depends on total distance traveled, which was not zero here.

options.text: Both their average speed and average velocity were equal and positive
options.feedback: Velocity depends on displacement, which is zero since they returned to the start.

options.text: Their average velocity was greater than their average speed
options.feedback: Velocity's magnitude can never exceed speed over the same time period.

easy.hard: One of these two quantities is a vector (has direction), the other is a scalar (magnitude only).
easy.medium: One of these terms tells you which way something is moving, not just how fast.
easy.easy: One of these words tells you both how fast AND which direction something moves.

medium.hard: Divide the total distance covered by the total time it took to cover it.
medium.medium: Divide 100 by 2 to find the speed.
medium.easy: Divide the distance by the time to get the speed.

hard.hard: Speed depends on total path length traveled, while velocity depends only on the net change in position (displacement) from start to finish.
hard.medium: The runner covered real ground (so speed isn't zero), but ended up exactly where they started (so displacement, and thus velocity, is zero).
hard.easy: The runner ran a real distance, but ended up back at the same spot -- so their overall position didn't change at all.

topic: types of energy: kinetic and potential

easy.text: What type of energy does a moving car have?

options.feedback: Correct -- kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Potential energy is stored energy due to position, not motion.
Nuclear energy comes from reactions within an atom's nucleus, unrelated to simply moving.
A moving car's main energy of interest here is due to its motion, not the sound it makes.

medium.text: A ball held high above the ground has what type of energy due to its position?

options.feedback: Correct -- height above the ground gives an object stored energy due to gravity.
Kinetic energy requires motion -- a held, stationary ball isn't moving.
Thermal energy relates to temperature/heat, not height.
There's no electric charge or current involved in simply holding a ball up.

hard.text: As a ball falls from a height, what happens to its kinetic and potential energy (ignoring air resistance)?

options.text: Potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases by the same amount
options.feedback: Correct -- total mechanical energy is conserved, so potential energy converts directly into kinetic energy as height decreases.

options.text: Both potential and kinetic energy increase together
options.feedback: Potential energy decreases as height decreases -- it doesn't increase alongside kinetic energy.

options.text: Both potential and kinetic energy decrease together
options.feedback: Kinetic energy actually increases as the ball speeds up while falling.

options.text: Energy simply disappears as the ball falls
options.feedback: Energy is conserved, not destroyed -- it converts from one form to another.

easy.hard: This form of energy depends directly on an object's speed.
easy.medium: This is the energy an object has because it's moving.
easy.easy: This is the energy something has just because it's moving.

medium.hard: This form of energy is stored due to an object's position relative to a force like gravity.
medium.medium: This is energy stored because of how high up something is.
medium.easy: This is the energy something has just because of how high up it is.

hard.hard: Without air resistance, total mechanical energy is conserved -- whatever height-based energy is lost converts directly into motion-based energy.
hard.medium: As height is lost, that stored energy transforms directly into energy of motion, keeping the total the same.
hard.easy: As the ball falls and loses height, that lost energy turns directly into speed -- the total amount stays the same.

options.feedback: Correct -- Ohm's law states V = I × R.
That relationship describes density, a completely different formula.
That's Newton's second law, not Ohm's law.
That's the basic motion formula, not Ohm's law.

medium.text: Using Ohm's law (V = I × R), what is the voltage across a resistor with 2 amps of current and 5 ohms of resistance?

options.feedback: Correct -- 2 × 5 = 10 volts.
This divides instead of multiplying current and resistance.
This adds current and resistance instead of multiplying them.
This doesn't match multiplying 2 by 5.

hard.text: If the resistance in a circuit doubles while the voltage stays constant, what happens to the current?

options.feedback: Correct -- since I = V/R, doubling R while V stays constant halves the current.
Current and resistance are inversely related when voltage is constant, so doubling resistance shouldn't double current.
Current depends directly on resistance in this formula, so it must change when resistance changes.
Doubling resistance reduces current, but doesn't eliminate it entirely.

easy.hard: This law connects electrical pressure, the flow of charge, and the opposition to that flow, all in one formula.
easy.medium: This law connects three electrical quantities in a circuit using one simple equation.
easy.easy: This law connects voltage, current, and resistance together.

medium.hard: Multiply the current value by the resistance value to find the voltage.
medium.medium: Multiply 2 by 5 to find the voltage.
medium.easy: Multiply the current and the resistance together.

hard.hard: Rearranging Ohm's law as I = V/R shows current is inversely proportional to resistance when voltage is held constant.
hard.medium: Since current equals voltage divided by resistance, increasing resistance while voltage stays fixed must decrease current proportionally.
hard.easy: If resistance doubles and voltage stays the same, the current has to drop -- specifically to half its original value.

easy.text: What is the distance between two consecutive crests of a wave called?

options.feedback: Correct -- wavelength measures the distance from one crest to the next.
Amplitude measures the height of the wave, not the distance between crests.
Frequency measures how many waves pass a point per second, not a distance.
Period measures time for one full wave cycle, not a spatial distance.

medium.text: What does the amplitude of a wave represent?

options.text: The maximum height of the wave from its resting position
options.feedback: Correct -- amplitude measures how far the wave displaces from equilibrium at its peak.

options.text: The number of waves passing a point each second
options.feedback: That describes frequency, not amplitude.

options.text: The speed at which the wave travels
options.feedback: That describes wave speed, a separate property from amplitude.
That describes wavelength, not amplitude.

hard.text: If a wave's frequency increases while its speed stays constant, what must happen to its wavelength?

options.feedback: Correct -- since speed = wavelength × frequency, keeping speed constant while frequency rises means wavelength must fall.
With speed fixed, a higher frequency requires a shorter wavelength, not a longer one.
Wavelength and frequency are linked through speed, so one changing while speed is fixed forces the other to change too.
The relationship (speed = wavelength × frequency) determines this precisely, it's not unknowable.

easy.hard: This measures a spatial gap, specifically between two identical repeating points on the wave.
easy.medium: This is the length of one complete wave cycle, from one peak to the next.
easy.easy: This measures how long one full wave 'loop' is, from peak to peak.

medium.hard: This measures how far the wave swings away from its neutral, undisturbed position at its most extreme point.
medium.medium: This is how tall or how far the wave reaches from its resting middle line.
medium.easy: This measures how big or tall the wave's peak is.

hard.hard: Speed equals wavelength times frequency -- if speed is fixed and frequency rises, wavelength must fall proportionally to keep the equation balanced.
hard.medium: Since speed = wavelength × frequency, and speed doesn't change, wavelength and frequency must move in opposite directions.
hard.easy: If speed stays the same and frequency goes up, wavelength has to go down to balance it out.

topic: states of matter and heat transfer

easy.text: What is the transfer of heat through direct contact between materials called?

options.feedback: Correct -- conduction is heat transfer through direct contact, like touching a hot pan.
Convection is heat transfer through the movement of fluids (liquids or gases), not direct contact.
Radiation is heat transfer through electromagnetic waves, without needing any contact at all.
Reflection describes light bouncing off a surface, not a method of heat transfer.

medium.text: Which method of heat transfer explains how the Sun warms the Earth, despite the vacuum of space between them?

options.feedback: Correct -- radiation travels as electromagnetic waves and doesn't require a physical medium.
Conduction requires direct contact between materials, which isn't possible across empty space.
Convection requires a fluid medium to carry heat, which space (a vacuum) doesn't have.
Friction requires two surfaces rubbing together, not applicable to sunlight crossing empty space.

hard.text: Which TWO of the following heat-transfer methods require a physical medium (matter) to occur?

options.feedback: Correct -- conduction relies on particle-to-particle contact within a material.
Correct -- convection relies on the physical movement of a fluid's particles.
Radiation travels through empty space and doesn't need any matter at all.

options.text: None of these require a medium
options.feedback: Two of the three listed methods do in fact require a physical medium.

easy.hard: This method requires the two objects to be physically touching each other.
easy.medium: This method needs direct physical contact between the two materials.
easy.easy: This is heat moving between two things that are physically touching.

medium.hard: This method travels as electromagnetic waves and can pass through the vacuum of empty space.
medium.medium: This is the only heat-transfer method that doesn't need any matter to travel through at all.
medium.easy: This type of heat transfer can travel through empty space, with nothing in between.

hard.hard: Two of the three rely on particles of matter interacting or moving to carry energy along; only one travels as waves with no particles required at all.
hard.medium: Two of these methods need actual particles of matter present to transfer the heat; one does not.
hard.easy: Two of these three need real matter to work; only one can travel through completely empty space.

easy.text: What is the formula for density?

options.feedback: Correct -- density equals mass divided by volume.
Density is found by dividing, not multiplying, these two quantities.
This is the inverse of density, not density itself.
Mass and volume have different units, so they can't simply be added together.

medium.text: An object has a mass of 20 grams and a volume of 4 cm³. What is its density?

options.feedback: Correct -- 20 divided by 4 equals 5.
This multiplies mass and volume instead of dividing.
This subtracts instead of dividing mass by volume.
This adds instead of dividing mass by volume.

hard.text: An object floats in water. What must be true about its density compared to water's density (1 g/cm³)?

options.text: The object's density is less than 1 g/cm³
options.feedback: Correct -- objects less dense than the fluid they're placed in will float.

options.text: The object's density is greater than 1 g/cm³
options.feedback: Objects denser than water sink rather than float.

options.text: The object's density is exactly 1 g/cm³
options.feedback: An object with exactly matching density would stay suspended in place, not float at the surface.

options.text: Density has no effect on whether something floats
options.feedback: Density relative to the fluid is precisely what determines floating versus sinking.

easy.hard: This property compares how much matter is packed into a given amount of space.
easy.medium: Divide how heavy something is by how much space it takes up.
easy.easy: Divide the mass by the volume to get this.

medium.hard: Divide the mass value by the volume value to compute density.
medium.medium: Divide 20 by 4 to find the density.
medium.easy: Divide the mass by the volume.

hard.hard: An object floats when it displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight while being less dense than that fluid overall.
hard.medium: Objects lighter than water for their size (less dense) will float; heavier-for-their-size (denser) ones sink.
hard.easy: Things that are less dense than water float; things denser than water sink.

easy.text: What is the fixed point that a lever pivots around called?

options.feedback: Correct -- the fulcrum is the fixed pivot point of a lever.
The load is the object being moved or lifted, not the pivot point.
Effort is the force applied to the lever, not the pivot point.
An axle is part of a wheel-and-axle machine, a different type of simple machine.

medium.text: Moving the fulcrum of a lever closer to the load generally has what effect?

options.text: It requires less effort force to lift the load
options.feedback: Correct -- a fulcrum closer to the load gives greater mechanical advantage, reducing the effort needed.

options.text: It requires more effort force to lift the load
options.feedback: Moving the fulcrum closer to the load actually makes lifting easier, not harder.

options.text: It has no effect on the effort needed
options.feedback: Fulcrum position directly changes the mechanical advantage of a lever.
The lever doesn't change the load's actual weight, only how much effort is needed to move it.

hard.text: A seesaw (a first-class lever) is balanced with a 40 kg child sitting 2 meters from the fulcrum. Where must a 20 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?

options.feedback: Correct -- balance requires equal torque: 40×2 = 20×4 = 80 on both sides.
At equal distance, the lighter child wouldn't balance the heavier one -- the torques wouldn't match.
This would produce far less torque than needed to balance the heavier child.
This produces more torque than needed, tipping the balance the other way.

easy.hard: This is the stationary point around which all rotation of the lever happens.
easy.medium: This is the point the lever rotates around, staying fixed in place.
easy.easy: This is the point where a lever balances and turns around.

medium.hard: Mechanical advantage in a lever increases as the fulcrum sits nearer to the resistance being moved.
medium.medium: The closer the pivot is to the heavy object, the easier it becomes to lift.
medium.easy: Moving the pivot point nearer to the heavy object makes it easier to lift.

hard.hard: Balance requires the product of weight and distance to be equal on both sides of the fulcrum -- solve for the distance that makes both sides match.
hard.medium: Multiply the first child's weight by their distance, then divide that result by the second child's weight to find their needed distance.
hard.easy: Multiply 40 by 2 to get 80, then figure out what distance times 20 also equals 80.
